questions.question: Explain the Fletcher checksum approach that is suitable for 8-bit and 16-bit checksum calculation.
questions.solution:
The Fletcher checksum was devised to weight each data item according to its position. Fletcher proposed two algorithms: 8-bit and 16-bit. The first, 8-bit Fletcher, calculates on 8-bit data items and creates a 16-bit checksum. The second, 16-bit Fletcher, calculates on 16-bit data items and creates a 32-bit checksum.
The 8-bit Fletcher is calculated over data octets (bytes) and creates a 16-bit checksum. The calculation is done modulo 256 (2^8), which means the intermediate results are divided by 256 and the remainder is kept. The algorithm uses two accumulators, L and R. The first simply adds data items together; the second adds a weight to the calculation.
The 16-bit Fletcher checksum is similar to the 8-bit Fletcher checksum, but it is calculated over 16-bit data items and creates a 32-bit checksum. The calculation is done modulo 65,536.
(Figure 10.18 flowchart: Start -> L = R = 0 -> R = (R + Di) mod 256 -> L = (L + R) mod 256 -> more data? loop -> Checksum = L x 256 + R -> Stop. Notes: L = left 8-bit checksum, R = right 8-bit checksum, Di = next 8-bit data item. The 16-bit checksum is the pair L | R.)

rubric.point: Fletcher weights each data item by its position; two variants exist, 8-bit and 16-bit
8-bit Fletcher works over octets and produces a 16-bit checksum, computed modulo 256
16-bit Fletcher works over 16-bit data items, produces a 32-bit checksum, modulo 65536
Flowchart of the algorithm: two accumulators L and R, R = (R + Di) mod 256, L = (L + R) mod 256, checksum = L x 256 + R

questions.question: A small research laboratory uses a switched Ethernet LAN. Two devices, Host A and Host B, are connected to the same Layer-2 network. Host A: IP address N1 and MAC address L1. Host B: IP address N2 and MAC address L2 (unknown to Host A initially). Host A needs to send an IP packet (payload belonging to an application layer message) to Host B. Identify the protocol used to initiate the transmission. Demonstrate with a diagram how the protocol Request is sent by Host A and the Reply packet by Host B, and also the contents of the request and reply protocol.
questions.solution:
The protocol is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol). ARP accepts an IP address from the IP protocol, maps the address to the corresponding link-layer address, and passes it to the data-link layer.
Anytime a host or a router needs to find the link-layer address of another host or router in its network, it sends an ARP request packet. The packet includes the link-layer and IP addresses of the sender and the IP address of the receiver. Because the sender does not know the link-layer address of the receiver, the query is broadcast over the link using the link-layer broadcast address.
(Diagram a: ARP request is broadcast - System A (N1, L1) broadcasts a request over the LAN, 'Looking for link-layer address of a node with IP address N2'. Diagram b: ARP reply is unicast - System B (N2, L2) replies 'I am the node and my link-layer address is L2'.)
(Packet contents: ARP request carries hardware type 0x0001, protocol type 0x0800, hardware length 0x06, protocol length 0x04, operation 0x0001; sender L1, N1; target All 0s, N2. It travels in a multicast/broadcast frame from A to B with destination B (broadcast address) and source A. ARP reply carries 0x0001, 0x0800, 0x06, 0x04, operation 0x0002; sender L2, N2; target L1, N1. It travels in a unicast frame from B to A with destination A and source B.)

rubric.point: Identifies the protocol as ARP, which maps an IP address to a link-layer (MAC) address
ARP request diagram: broadcast over the LAN carrying sender L1/N1 and target N2 with an all-zero target hardware address, operation 0x0001
ARP reply diagram: unicast from B back to A carrying L2/N2 as sender and L1/N1 as target, operation 0x0002

questions.question: Compare and contrast byte-oriented and bit-oriented protocols. Apply bit stuffing to bit-stuff the following frame payload: 0001111111001111101000111111111110000111. Unstuff the following frame payload: 0001111100000111110111010011101111100000 1111.
questions.solution:
In character-oriented (or byte-oriented) framing, data to be carried are 8-bit characters from a coding system such as ASCII. The header, which normally carries the source and destination addresses and other control information, and the trailer, which carries error detection redundant bits, are also multiples of 8 bits. To separate one frame from the next, an 8-bit (1-byte) flag is added at the beginning and the end of a frame.

In bit-oriented framing, the data section of a frame is a sequence of bits to be interpreted by the upper layer as text, graphic, audio, video, and so on. However, in addition to headers (and possible trailers), we still need a delimiter to separate one frame from the other. Most protocols use a special 8-bit pattern flag, 01111110, as the delimiter to define the beginning and the end of the frame.

Bit stuffing (whenever five consecutive 1s appear, insert a 0 after them):
0001111101110001111100100001111101111010000111

Bit unstuffing (scan for the pattern 11111 followed by 0 and remove that 0). After removing every stuffed 0, the unstuffed sequence becomes:
0001111100000111111110100110111110000011 11
questions.breakdown_text: Character-oriented framing 1M, bit-oriented framing 1M, bit stuffing 1.5M, bit unstuffing 1.5M

rubric.point: Character/byte-oriented framing: data are 8-bit characters (e.g. ASCII), header and trailer are multiples of 8 bits, and an 8-bit flag delimits the frame
Bit-oriented framing: the data section is an arbitrary sequence of bits, delimited by the 8-bit flag pattern 01111110
Bit stuffing: after five consecutive 1s insert a 0, applied correctly across the given payload
Bit unstuffing: scan for 11111 followed by 0 and remove that 0, applied correctly across the given payload

steps: Bit stuffing: scan left to right and insert a 0 after every five consecutive 1s
Bit unstuffing: scan for five consecutive 1s followed by a 0, and delete that 0
method.carry_forward: Mark the rule and whether it was applied consistently. A single missed insertion or deletion in a long bit string is a slip, not a wrong method, and should not void the item.

questions.question: Identify the media access protocol where the stations consult one another to find which station has the right to access the medium. Demonstrate with neat diagrams the protocol where the primary station has all the control of the medium access.
questions.solution:
In controlled access, the stations consult one another to find which station has the right to send. A station cannot send unless it has been authorized by other stations.

Polling works with topologies in which one device is designated as a primary station and the other devices are secondary stations. All data exchanges must be made through the primary device even when the ultimate destination is a secondary device. The primary device controls the link; the secondary devices follow its instructions. It is up to the primary device to determine which device is allowed to use the channel at a given time.

(Diagram: (a) Select - Primary sends SEL, secondary replies ACK, primary sends Data, secondary replies ACK. (b) Poll - Primary sends Poll, secondary replies NAK if it has nothing; primary polls the next, which replies Data, and the primary returns ACK.)

Select: the select function is used whenever the primary device has something to send. The primary controls the link. If the primary is neither sending nor receiving data, it knows the link is available. If it has something to send, the primary device sends it. What it does not know, however, is whether the target device is prepared to receive. So the primary must alert the secondary to the upcoming transmission and wait for an acknowledgment of the secondary's ready status. Before sending data, the primary creates and transmits a select (SEL) frame, one field of which includes the address of the intended secondary.

Poll: the poll function is used by the primary device to solicit transmissions from the secondary devices. When the primary is ready to receive data, it must ask (poll) each device in turn if it has anything to send. When the first secondary is approached, it responds either with a NAK frame if it has nothing to send or with data (in the form of a data frame) if it does. If the response is negative (a NAK frame), then the primary polls the next secondary in the same manner until it finds one with data to send. When the response is positive (a data frame), the primary reads the frame and returns an acknowledgment (ACK frame), verifying its receipt.

rubric.point: Identifies controlled access, and polling as the protocol where a primary station controls medium access
Diagram of select and poll exchanges between primary and secondaries
Select: primary has data to send, sends a SEL frame naming the intended secondary and waits for an ACK confirming readiness before sending data
Poll: primary asks each secondary in turn; a secondary replies NAK if it has nothing or a data frame if it has, and the primary returns an ACK

questions.question: A digital communication system uses NRZ-I and Manchester line coding schemes to transfer 10-Mbps data. (a) Calculate the average signal rate and minimum bandwidth for both the schemes. (b) Draw the NRZ-I and Manchester waveform for the bit sequence 1011001. (c) Analyze the behaviour of both schemes with respect to baseline wandering and self synchronization.
questions.solution:
(a) Average signal rate S = c x N x (1/r).
NRZ-I: c = 1/2, r = 1, so Savg = N/2 = 5 Mbaud, and the minimum bandwidth Bmin = N/2 = 5 MHz.
Manchester: c = 1, r = 1/2, so Savg = N = 10 Mbaud, and Bmin = N = 10 MHz.

(b) Waveforms for 1011001. NRZ-I: the signal inverts at the start of a bit when the bit is 1, and holds its level when the bit is 0 (next bit 0 -> no transition, next bit 1 -> invert the previous level). Manchester: every bit has a mid-bit transition - 0 is high-to-low and 1 is low-to-high - which also carries the clock.

(c) In NRZ-I the baseline wandering problem occurs only for a long sequence of 0s. If we can eliminate the long sequence of 0s, we can avoid baseline wandering. In NRZ-I the synchronization problem also exists for a long sequence of 0s, which can cause a problem in NRZ-I. In Manchester there is no baseline wandering and no synchronization problem, because the guaranteed mid-bit transition provides both a self-clocking signal and a balanced average level.
questions.breakdown_text: Part A 2 + 2M, Part B 2 + 2M, Part C 1 + 1M
questions.transcription_note: The (a) panel is a faint handwritten insert. The Manchester line (Savg = N = 10 Mbaud, Bmin = N = 10 MHz) is legible. The NRZ-I figures are not cleanly legible; the values recorded here (N/2 = 5 Mbaud, Bmin = 5 MHz) are the standard result for N = 10 Mbps and are consistent with the c = 1/2 factor written beside them. Confirm against the original before using this sub-item to fail a student.

rubric.point: NRZ-I: average signal rate = N/2 = 5 Mbaud and minimum bandwidth = 5 MHz
Manchester: average signal rate = N = 10 Mbaud and minimum bandwidth = 10 MHz
NRZ-I waveform for 1011001: level inverts on a 1 and holds on a 0
Manchester waveform for 1011001: a mid-bit transition in every bit, 0 high-to-low and 1 low-to-high
Baseline wandering: a problem in NRZ-I for long runs of 0s; absent in Manchester
Self-synchronization: NRZ-I loses sync over long runs of 0s; Manchester is self-synchronizing thanks to the guaranteed mid-bit transition

steps: Average signal rate S = c x N x (1/r)
For NRZ-I, c = 1/2 and r = 1, so S = N/2
For Manchester, c = 1 and r = 1/2, so S = N
Minimum bandwidth equals the average signal rate for both schemes
method.carry_forward: If the student uses a wrong c or r, mark the bandwidth step on the signal rate they themselves computed.

questions.question: i) Describe the working of the CSMA/CD protocol with example. ii) Assume that there are only two stations, A and B, in a bus CSMA/CD network. The distance between the two stations is 2000 m and the propagation speed is 2 x 10^8 m/s. If station A starts transmitting at time t1: (a) Analyze if the protocol allows station B to start transmitting at time t1 + 8 us? If the answer is yes, justify. (b) Analyze if the protocol allows station B to start transmitting at time t1 + 11 us? If the answer is yes, justify.
questions.solution:
i) The CSMA method does not specify the procedure following a collision. Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD) augments the algorithm to handle the collision. In this method, a station monitors the medium after it sends a frame to see if the transmission was successful. If so, the station is finished. If, however, there is a collision, the frame is sent again.
(Diagram: stations A, B, C, D on a bus. At time t1, station A has executed its persistence procedure and starts sending the bits of its frame. At time t2, station C has not yet sensed the first bit sent by A. Station C executes its persistence procedure and starts sending the bits in its frame, which propagate both to the left and to the right. The collision occurs some time after time t2. Station C detects a collision at time t3 when it receives the first bit of A's frame, and immediately aborts transmission. Station A detects the collision at time t4 when it receives the first bit of C's frame, and also immediately aborts transmission. A transmits for the duration t4 - t1; C transmits for the duration t3 - t2.)

ii) One-way propagation delay = distance / speed = 2000 m / (2 x 10^8 m/s) = 0.00001 s = 10 us. So A's first bit reaches B at t1 + 10 us.

(a) If B starts at t1 + 8 us: at that instant the signal from A has not yet arrived at B (it arrives at t1 + 10 us). So B senses the channel idle and is allowed by CSMA to start transmitting. When A's signal arrives at B at t1 + 10 us it collides with B's transmission. B detects the collision immediately on arrival of A's signal (at t1 + 10 us), sends a jam and aborts. A will detect the collision only after B's transmission (or jam) propagates back to A: B started at t1 + 8 us, so B's earliest signal reaches A at t1 + 8 + 10 = t1 + 18 us. So A detects the collision at about t1 + 18 us. Both stations then follow the CSMA/CD collision-handling procedure (jam, stop, wait a random backoff, retransmit).

(b) If B starts at t1 + 11 us: at that instant A's signal has already arrived at B (it arrived at t1 + 10 us). Therefore B senses the channel busy and must defer - CSMA does not allow B to start transmitting then. So no collision occurs; B waits until it senses the channel idle (i.e. after A's transmission and propagation effects end) before attempting to transmit.

rubric.point: CSMA/CD timing diagram showing A and C transmitting, the collision, and both stations aborting
Explanation: a station monitors the medium after sending; on a collision it aborts and resends. A transmits for t4 - t1 and C for t3 - t2
(a) Propagation delay is 2000 / (2 x 10^8) = 10 us, so at t1 + 8 us B still senses idle and IS allowed to transmit; the collision then occurs at t1 + 10 us at B and A learns of it at about t1 + 18 us
(b) At t1 + 11 us A's signal has already arrived, so B senses the channel busy, defers, and is NOT allowed to transmit; no collision occurs

steps: Propagation delay = distance / propagation speed
A's first bit reaches B one propagation delay after A starts
B may begin only if it senses the channel idle at that instant
A learns of the collision one further propagation delay after B starts
method.carry_forward: Both sub-parts hang on the propagation delay. If that figure is wrong but the idle/busy reasoning is applied correctly to it, mark both parts on the student's own value.

questions.question: A virtual-circuit connection must be established between host A and host B through two switches, S1 and S2. Link A->S1: bandwidth 2 Mbps, distance 600 m. Link S1->S2: bandwidth 1.5 Mbps, distance 1200 m. Link S2->B: bandwidth 4 Mbps, distance 400 m. Packet size for all packets (setup, ack, data, teardown) is 500 bytes. Speed of signal in copper/fiber = 2 x 10^8 m/s. Switch processing delay S1: 1 ms, S2: 1.5 ms. One data packet of 500 bytes is sent. Compute i) round-trip setup delay ii) per packet delay iii) total end-to-end time.
questions.solution:
A 500-byte packet is 4000 bits.
Transmission delay = packet size / bandwidth:
A->S1: 4000 / (2 x 10^6) = 2 ms
S1->S2: 4000 / (1.5 x 10^6) = 2.67 ms
S2->B: 4000 / (4 x 10^6) = 1 ms

Propagation delay = distance / speed:
A->S1: 600 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.003 ms
S1->S2: 1200 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.006 ms
S2->B: 400 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.002 ms

i) Round-trip setup delay = 2 x [ sum(Tt + Tp) + S1 processing + S2 processing ]
= 2 x [ (2 + 0.003) + (2.67 + 0.006) + (1 + 0.002) + 1 + 1.5 ]
= 2 x 8.181 = 16.362 ms

ii) Per packet delay (data transmission one way) = sum(Tt + Tp)
= (2 + 0.003) + (2.67 + 0.006) + (1 + 0.002) = 5.681 ms per packet

iii) Total end-to-end time = round-trip setup + data transfer + teardown
= 16.362 + 5.681 + 8.181 = 30.224 ms
questions.breakdown_text: Transmission delay calculation 2M, propagation delay calculation 2M, i) 2M, ii) 2M, iii) 2M
questions.transcription_note: The solution panel is a photographed handwritten sheet. The three headline answers (16.362 ms, 5.681 ms, 30.224 ms) are legible and arithmetically consistent with the stated link parameters, which is how they were verified.

rubric.point: Transmission delays: 2 ms, 2.67 ms and 1 ms for the three links (500 bytes = 4000 bits)
Propagation delays: 0.003 ms, 0.006 ms and 0.002 ms
Round-trip setup delay = 2 x 8.181 = 16.362 ms, including both switch processing delays
Per packet delay = 5.681 ms
Total end-to-end time = 16.362 + 5.681 + 8.181 = 30.224 ms

steps: Transmission delay = packet size in bits / link bandwidth, for each of the three links
Propagation delay = distance / signal speed, for each link
Round-trip setup = 2 x (sum of transmission + propagation over all links + both switch processing delays)
Per packet delay = sum of transmission + propagation one way
Total end-to-end = setup + data transfer + teardown
method.carry_forward: Every headline figure is built from the per-link delays. If a per-link delay is wrong but the three sums are formed correctly, award the setup, per-packet and total steps on the student's own numbers.

questions.question: A sender wants to transmit the dataword 1101011011 using Cyclic Redundancy Check CRC(n,k). The generator polynomial is represented by the bit pattern 10011. (a) Determine the number of bits in the codeword and redundant bits. Write the augmented message used for division. (b) Perform the CRC binary division and compute the remainder. (c) Determine the final transmitted frame (dataword + CRC). (d) Demonstrate how the receiver verifies whether the received frame contains an error if the MSB is flipped.
questions.solution:
CRC(n,k): the generator 10011 has degree 4, so r = 4 redundant bits. The dataword has k = 10 bits, so the codeword has n = k + r = 14 bits. This is CRC(14,10).

(a) Append 4 zeros to the dataword to form the augmented message: 11010110110000.

(b) Binary division of 11010110110000 by 10011 (XOR at each aligned 1):
Step 1 - align the divisor at position 0 and XOR: dividend 11010110110000, divisor 10011, result 01001110110000.
Step 2 - next 1 at position 2, XOR again: dividend 01001110110000, divisor 10011 shifted, result 00000010110000.
Step 3 - next 1 at position 6, XOR: dividend 00000010110000, divisor 10011 shifted, result 00000000101000.
Step 4 - next 1 at position 8, XOR: dividend 00000000101000, divisor 10011 shifted, result 00000000001110.
Remainder = last 4 bits = 1110.

(c) Final transmitted frame = dataword + remainder = 1101011011 1110 = 11010110111110.

(d) The receiver divides the received frame by the same generator 10011. If the remainder is 0000 there is no error. For the correctly received frame here the remainder is 0000. If the MSB is flipped the received frame becomes 01010110111110; dividing that by 10011 gives a non-zero remainder, so the receiver detects the error and discards the frame.
questions.verified: The remainder 1110 and the transmitted frame 11010110111110 were recomputed independently and match the scheme.

rubric.point: Binary division by 10011 carried out by repeated XOR, giving remainder 1110
Transmitted frame = 11010110111110
Receiver divides the received frame by 10011; a zero remainder means no error, and flipping the MSB gives a non-zero remainder so the error is detected

steps: r = the degree of the generator, k = dataword length, n = k + r
Append r zeros to the dataword to form the augmented message
Divide by the generator, XOR-ing at each aligned leading 1
The remainder is the last r bits
Transmitted frame = dataword followed by the remainder
The receiver divides the received frame by the same generator; a zero remainder means no error
method.carry_forward: The frame and the receiver check both follow from the remainder. If the division goes wrong but the append, the frame assembly and the verification procedure are right, award those steps on the student's own remainder.
